en: The exponents of Brahman say: What is the cause? What is Brahman? From whence have we been born?
By what do we live, and upon what are we established? By whom are we governed as we abide in pleasure and pain?
Tell us this, O Knower of Brahman, according to the established order.
Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, and the person— these are to be considered as the causes;
it is their conjunction that produces existence, not from the self-nature of a soul.
For the self is not the master over the cause of pleasure and pain. 1.2.
Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities—
that [power] which [is the source] of all those causes.
The One presides over those things joined with time and the self. || 1.3 ||
That [wheel] has one felly, is threefold, ends in sixteen,
has fifty spokes, and twenty counter-spokes;
it has six groups of eight and a single noose of manifold forms.
The division of the three paths, the two causes, and the single delusion. || 1.4 ||
It has five streams of water, five wombs as its fierce mouths, five vital breaths as its waves, and the five faculties of cognition as its root;
it possesses five whirlpools and the forceful current of the fivefold flood of suffering.
We study [it] as having fifty divisions and five sections. || 1.5 ||
In that vast wheel of Brahman, which is the source of all livelihoods and the support of all things, the *haṃsa* (the individual soul) revolves;
having perceived the Self as distinct from the Impeller, [one attains liberation].
Being thus delighted by him, he then attains immortality. || 1.6 ||
This supreme Brahman is indeed sung as the Udgītha; within it, the triad and the imperishable are well-established.
Having realized the interval therein, the knowers of Brahman [attain liberation].
Absorbed in Brahman and devoted to it, they are liberated from the womb. || 1.7 ||
The Lord sustains this entire universe— the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest—
joined together; yet the self, though not the Lord, is bound by its state as an enjoyer.
Having known the God, one is released from all fetters.
The two, the Knower and the Unknowing, are unborn—the Lord and the Non-Lord;
for the Unborn is one, joined with the objects of enjoyment for the enjoyer;
and the Self is infinite, universal in form, and indeed a non-doer.
When one finds this triad, that is Brahman. || 1.9 ||
The perishable is the primary matter (pradhāna), and the imperishable immortal is Hara;
the one God rules over both the perishable and the self.
Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through the realization of His true nature—
And furthermore, at the end, there is the cessation of all illusion. || 1.10 ||
Having known the God, there is the falling away of all bonds;
with the afflictions destroyed, there is the abandonment of birth and death. By meditating upon Him, after the dissolution of the body, [the third state is attained].
Possessing universal sovereignty, he is absolute and one whose desires are fulfilled. || 1.11 ||
This should be known as eternally established in the Self; indeed, there is nothing further to be known beyond this.

Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller— The final verse is: Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller, the wise man, having known all that is to be known, is not born again.
All this that has been declared is the threefold Brahman. || 1.12 ||
Just as the form of fire, when it has entered its source, is not seen and yet its characteristic mark is not destroyed,
so it is again perceived when it is grasped within the source of its fuel.
Both of these, indeed, [are established] in the body by means of the syllable Om.
Making one's own body the lower fire-drill and the Praṇava the upper fire-drill, one shall behold the God hidden within, through the practice of the friction of meditation. 1.14
As oil is in sesame seeds, as butter is in curds, as water is in riverbeds, and as fire is in the kindling woods—
so is this Self grasped within the self.
He who perceives this through truth and austerity. || 1.15 ||
The Self, all-pervading, is contained within like ghee in milk;
it has as its root the knowledge of the Self and austerity—that is the supreme Upaniṣad of Brahman, that is the supreme Upaniṣad of Brahman. 1.16
Thus ends the first chapter.
Harnessing his mind for the first time and fixing his thoughts upon reality, Savitṛ, having perceived Agni as the light, brought him forth from the earth. 2.1.
With a disciplined mind, we [act] at the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with power for the sake of attaining the heavenly world. 2.2.
Having yoked the gods with his mind, as they proceed toward the sun through inspired thought to heaven, Savitar impels them as they are about to create the great light. 2.3.
The inspired poets harness their minds and harness their thoughts for the sake of the great, inspired, wise one; he alone, the knower of the sacred ways, ordains the priestly offices.
Great is the praise of the divine Savitṛ. 2.4.
I yoke for you both an ancient prayer with prostrations;
let the hymn go forth like a traveler on the path of the patron.
All the sons of immortality listen.
Those who have taken their stand in the divine abodes. || 2.5 ||
Where fire is churned forth, where the wind is obstructed, and where the moon overflows—there the mind is born. (2.6)
May he enjoy the ancient prayer through the impulse of Savitṛ;
there you shall prepare a womb for him, for your bounty has not failed. 2.7.
Having established the body evenly with the three [upper parts] raised,
and having withdrawn the senses into the heart by means of the mind,
the wise one should cross over by means of the raft of Brahman.
All streams bring fear. || 2.8 ||
Having restrained his vital breaths here through disciplined effort,
he should breathe through the nostrils when the breath has subsided;
for this [body] is like a vehicle yoked to vicious horses.
The wise man, being vigilant, should fix his mind. || 2.9 ||
In a clean place, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, devoid of noise and water sources,
agreeable to the mind and not distressing to the eyes.
One should employ [this practice] while taking refuge in a cave sheltered from the wind. || 2.10 ||
These forms— mist, smoke, sun, fire, wind, firefly, lightning, crystal, and moon—
are the precursors.
In yoga, these bring about the manifestation of Brahman.
When the fivefold quality of yoga has arisen from earth, water, fire, air, and space, and is fully operative,
for him there is no disease, no old age, and no death.
The body of one who has attained [this state] consists of the fire of yoga. || 2.12 ||
Lightness, health, freedom from greed, clarity of complexion, excellence of voice,
a pleasant odor, and scanty urine and feces.
They say that the first stage is the engagement in yoga. || 2.13 ||
Just as a statue coated with clay shines forth when it is well-burnished and filled with light,
so too does the embodied being shine after having clearly perceived that reality of the Self.
One becomes fulfilled and free from sorrow. || 2.14 ||
But when one who is disciplined here beholds the reality of Brahman through the reality of the Self— comparable to a lamp—
as unborn, eternal, and purified of all principles;
Having known the God, one is released from all bonds. || 2.15 ||
This god indeed pervades all the quarters; he was born first, and he is within the womb.
He is the one already born, and he is the one yet to be born.
He stands facing each person, with faces on every side.
The god who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who has entered the entire world, who is in the plants, and who is in the trees—to that god, salutation after salutation. 2.17
Thus ends the second chapter.
He who alone, possessing a net, rules with his ruling powers, rules all worlds with his ruling powers;
he who alone exists at both emergence and dissolution.
Those who know this become immortal. 3.1.
For there is only one Rudra; he does not stand for a second.
He who rules these worlds by his ruling powers stands facing all people; at the time of the end, he draws himself together.
Having brought all worlds together, he is the guardian.
With eyes on every side and faces on every side, with arms on every side and feet on every side,
he blows forth with his two arms and with his wings.
The one God, generating heaven and earth. 3.3.
He who is the source and origin of the gods, the sovereign of all, Rudra the great seer,
brought forth Hiraṇyagarbha in the beginning.
May he endow us with auspicious understanding. 3.4.
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible and does not appear evil—with that most peaceful form, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with favor. 3.5.
O Lord of the Mountain, O Protector of the Mountain, that arrow which you carry in your hand to discharge—make it auspicious; do not harm the person or the world.
Beyond that, [he saw] the Supreme Brahman, the Great One,
hidden within all beings according to their respective classes,
the one who encompasses the universe.
Having known that Lord, they become immortal. 3.7
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent as the sun, beyond darkness;
only by knowing him does one pass over death.
There is no other path for reaching [the goal]. 3.8.
Than whom there is nothing further,
than whom there is nothing smaller or greater;
like an immovable tree, He alone stands in heaven.
Therefore, all this is filled by the Puruṣa. || 3.9 ||
Then, that which is higher than this, which is formless and free from ailment— those who know this become immortal, while others enter only into suffering. 3.10.
Having all faces, heads, and necks, dwelling in the secret cave of all beings, that Blessed One is all-pervading; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent. 3.11
The Great Lord, the Puruṣa, is indeed the instigator of this existence;
the imperishable Light, the Sovereign, has attained this utterly stainless state.
The Person the size of a thumb, the inner self,
is eternally seated within the hearts of people;
he is fashioned by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind.
Those who know this become immortal. 3.13
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
having pervaded the earth on all sides, he stood beyond it by the measure of ten fingers. 3.14
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be; moreover, he is the lord of immortality, which surpasses that which grows by food. 3.15
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and with ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all. 3.16.
Manifesting the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses;
the Lord and Ruler of all, the vast refuge of all. 3.17
In the city of nine gates, the embodied soul, like a swan, flutters outside;
it is the master of the entire world, both the stationary and the moving. (3.18)
Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper;
without eyes, he sees; without ears, he hears.
He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him.
They call him the foremost, the great Person. || 3.19 ||
Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great,
the Self is hidden in the cave of this living being;
one who is free from sorrow beholds that desireless One.
The majesty and lordship [arise] from the clarity of the elements. || 3.20 ||
I know this unaging, ancient one,
the Self of all, who is omnipresent by virtue of his pervasiveness—
he whose birth and cessation they proclaim.
For those who discourse on Brahman always proclaim this. || 3.21 ||
Thus ends the third chapter.

He who, being one and colorless, through the application of his power, bestows many colors while containing all meanings within himself; he who pervades the universe at the end and at the beginning—that God may endow us with auspicious intelligence. 4.1.
That indeed is Agni, that is Āditya, that is Vāyu, and that is Candramas;
that indeed is Śukra, that is Brahman, that is the Waters, and that is Prajāpati. 4.2.
You are woman, you are man; you are the youth and also the maiden. You, as an old man, totter along with a staff; you are born with faces turned in every direction. 4.3.
Blue is the winged one, green, red-eyed; he contains lightning within him; he is the seasons and the oceans.
You are beginningless and exist through your pervasive power, from whom all the worlds have been born. 4.4
There is one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form;
one unborn male, taking pleasure in her, lies by her, while another unborn male abandons her after he has enjoyed his enjoyment. (4.5)
Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating. 4.6.
On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by a lack of sovereignty;
but when he perceives Him who is adored as the other, the Lord, and His majesty, then he is freed from sorrow. 4.7.

In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods are seated—if one does not know that, what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they sit here together. 4.8.

The Vedas, sacrifices, rituals, and vows; the past, the future, and whatever the Vedas declare—this entire universe the Illusionist creates, and within it another is bound by that very illusion. (4.9)
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial matter) and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā;
by his constituent parts, indeed, this entire world is pervaded. 4.10

He who alone presides over every womb, in whom this entire universe comes together and dissolves—having perceived that Lord, the boon-granting God, worthy of praise, one attains this ultimate peace. 4.11
May he who is the source and origin of the gods, the sovereign of all, Rudra the great seer—may he, beholding Hiraṇyagarbha as he is being born, endow us with auspicious wisdom. 4.12.
He who is the sovereign lord of the gods, upon whom the worlds are supported, he who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? 4.13.

Having known Him who is subtler than the subtlest, the creator of the manifold world in its midst, the one who encompasses the universe—having known that auspicious One, he attains ultimate peace. (4.14)
He alone is the protector of the world at all times, the sovereign of all, hidden within all beings;
knowing Him thus—He in whom the Brahman-sages and the deities are united—one cuts the bonds of death. 4.15.
Having known Śiva, who is subtler than the cream atop clarified butter, hidden within all beings, and having known the God as the one who envelops the universe, one is released from all bonds. (4.16)
This divine Viśvakarman, the Great Soul, is eternally seated within the hearts of all people.
Fashioned by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind—those who know this become immortal. 4.17
When there was darkness, then there was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone was absolute.
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ, and from it the ancient wisdom issued forth. 4.18.
Neither above, nor across, nor in the middle can one grasp him; there is no likeness of him whose name is Great Renown. 4.19
His form does not stand within the range of sight; no one beholds him with the eye. Those who know him thus, abiding in the heart by means of the heart and the mind, become immortal. 4.20.
Thinking "He is unborn," a certain fearful person takes refuge in Rudra;
with that face of yours which is turned to the south, protect me always. 4.21.
Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, nor in our life-span; do not harm us in our cattle or our horses.
O Rudra, do not slay our heroes in your wrath. Bearing oblations, we invoke you forever. 4.22.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
In the infinite city of Brahman, two syllables—knowledge and ignorance—are hidden;
therein, ignorance is the perishable, while knowledge is indeed the immortal. He who rules over both knowledge and ignorance is another. 5.1.
He who alone presides over every womb, over all forms and all wombs; he who, at the beginning, sustains with his powers Kapila, born of the Rishis, and beholds him as he is being born. (5.2)
Transforming each individual net manifoldly, this God withdraws it into this field;
having created it again, the Lord likewise causes it to fall, and the Great-Souled One exercises sovereign mastery over all.
Just as the sun shines, illuminating all directions—above, below, and across—so does that divine, venerable Lord, the one, preside over the natures of all sources of birth. 5.4
He who, as the source of the universe, ripens his own nature and transforms all things that are to be ripened;
he alone presides over this entire world and assigns all the qualities their respective functions. (5.5)
That which is hidden in the secret Upaniṣads of the Vedas—Brahmā knows that as the source of Brahman.
Those ancient gods and sages who knew it became truly immortal, being absorbed in that very essence.

He who is associated with the qualities (guṇas), who is the agent of actions and the fruits thereof, and who is the enjoyer of what has been done—he, whose form is the universe, consisting of the three qualities and following the three paths, moves about as the lord of the vital breaths by means of his own actions. (5.7)

The one who is the size of a thumb, whose form is like the sun, and who is endowed with volition and egoism; by means of the quality of the intellect and the quality of the self, he is seen as even smaller than the tip of an awl. (5.8)
The individual soul (jīva) should be known as a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, further divided into a hundred parts; yet it is capable of infinity. 5.9
This is neither female nor male, nor indeed is it neuter;
whatever body it assumes, by that it is joined.

Through delusions of imagination, touch, and sight, and by means of food, water, and rain, the embodied soul undergoes birth and growth; following its past actions, it sequentially assumes various forms in different states of existence. (5.11)
The embodied soul assumes many forms, both gross and subtle, through its own qualities;
moreover, another cause for their conjunction is observed, consisting of the qualities of action and the qualities of the self. (5.12)

Having known the God who is without beginning or end, situated in the midst of the chaotic mass, the creator of the universe and manifold in form, the one who encompasses the universe—he is released from all bonds. (5.13)

Those who know the God—who is perceivable through meditative absorption, called the "nestless," the auspicious cause of both existence and non-existence, and the creator of the emanation of the *kalās*—they have abandoned the body. 5.14
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Some poets speak of inherent nature, while others, being utterly deluded, speak of time;
yet this is the majesty of the Divine in the world, by which this wheel of Brahma is made to revolve.
By him indeed all this is eternally pervaded—he who is the knower, the maker of time, possessed of qualities, and the possessor of all knowledge;
impelled by him, the action consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and space revolves; thus it should be reflected upon.

Having performed that action and turned back from it once more, he attains union with reality through reality itself—by means of one, two, three, or eight [disciplines], as well as by time and his own subtle qualities. (6.3)

He who initiates actions endowed with qualities and employs all states of being—when those [states] cease to exist, his performed actions perish; upon the exhaustion of action, he passes away as something essentially other. (6.4)

Having first worshipped that primordial God, who is the cause of the motive for conjunction, who is seen as beyond the three times though himself timeless, who is the universal form, the source of existence, and worthy of praise—residing within one's own mind; (6.5)
He is beyond and other than this phenomenal world which revolves through the forms of trees, time, and shapes;
having known Him as the bringer of dharma, the dispeller of evil, the Lord of Fortune, the immortal Self-abiding one, and the abode of the universe—6.6.
Let us know him as the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme divinity among deities, the supreme lord among lords—the adorable God, the Lord of the world, who stands beyond all. 6.7.
For him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither one equal to him nor superior to him is seen.
His supreme power is heard of as truly manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are inherent. 6.8
He has no master in the world, nor any ruler, nor even any mark; he is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and there is no progenitor for him, nor any overlord. (6.9)
May that one God, who by his own nature veils himself with the products of primordial matter as if with threads on a swift-spinning wheel, grant us absorption into Brahman. 6.10

One God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings; the supervisor of actions, the dwelling place of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, solitary and devoid of qualities. 6.11.
The one controller of the many inactive ones, who makes the single seed manifold—those wise ones who perceive Him abiding within themselves attain eternal happiness, and no others. 6.12.

The eternal among the eternals, the consciousness of the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of the many—having known that Cause, the God who is to be attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, one is released from all fetters. 6.13.
There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire.
Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined. 6.14
There is but one swan in the midst of this world; he alone is the fire seated within the waters.
Knowing him alone, one goes beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. 6.15
He is the maker of all, the knower of all, self-born, the conscious one, the fashioner of time, possessed of attributes, and the master of all knowledge;

he is the lord of both primary matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (kṣetrajña), the master of the qualities (guṇas), and the cause of bondage, maintenance, and liberation from the cycle of existence.
Consisting of that, immortal, established in the Lord, the knower, all-pervading, the protector of this world—he who eternally rules over this universe;
no other cause exists for his lordship.
He who first creates Brahmā and indeed imparts the Vedas to him.
I, desiring liberation, indeed take refuge in that God who is the light of self-knowledge. 6.18
Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless;
the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed. (6.19)
When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then, without having known the Divine, there will be an end to suffering. 6.20.

Then the wise Śvetāśvatara, through the power of his austerity and by the grace of the gods, fully proclaimed to those beyond the stages of life this supreme purifier, which is cherished by the assembly of sages. (6.21)
This supreme secret of the Vedānta, which was proclaimed in a former age, must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor again to one who is not a son or a disciple. (6.22)

For that great-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and who regards the teacher as he does the Divine—for him these truths thus explained truly shine forth; they shine forth for the great-souled one. 6.23.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Thus ends the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.
